OUTLINE VIEW
Pretest
Discover What You Know
Learning Objectives
Interpret the pathophysiology of spinal muscular atrophy.
Assess orthopaedic manifestations of spinal muscular atrophy.
Determine biologic interventions for spinal muscular atrophy that are changing the natural
history of the disease.
Pathophysiology/Pathoanatomy
Overview
Spinal muscular atrophy (SMA) is a genetic disease that is most commonly fatal during
childhood.
Incidence of 1 in 11,000 live births
The inheritance pattern of SMA is primarily autosomal recessive.



Progressive weakness starts proximally and moves distally through the body.
Epidemiology
Approximately 1 in 50 Americans is a carrier of SMA.
Etiology
Mutations in the survival motor neuron 1 (SMN1) gene on chromosome 5q cause deficiency of
the SMN protein, resulting in progressive loss of alpha-motor neurons in the anterior horn of
the spinal cord and progressive weakness.

Etiology
Ninety-six percent of SMA is caused by a deletion in exon 7 or 8 of SMN1, with a 2% de
novo deletion rate. Two genes, SMN1 and SMN2, both at 5q13, are involved in the
occurrence of SMA. They code for the SMN protein; however, SMN2 codes for a less
functional SMN protein. All patients with SMA lack both copies of SMN1, and the severity
of SMA is thought to be determined by the number of functional copies of the SMN2
gene. Healthy individuals have two SMA2 gene copies. In patients with SMA, the mutation
in SMN1 can functionally convert it to SMN2. Patients with SMA can have up to four
functional copies. The more functional copies of SMA2 that are present, the less severe
the phenotypic expression; however, exceptions to the disease severity correlation to
SMN2 exist. Protein expression of SMN concentrates in the nervous system and is
believed to be involved in dendrite and axon development.
Natural History
Individuals with type 0 to type 2 SMA have a shortened life expectancy.
Children often succumb to respiratory failure because of restrictive lung disease,
hypoventilation, and a weak cough.1,2
Individuals with type 3 or type 4 SMA have a similar life expectancy to the general population.

2/15

Classification
Type 0 SMA
Type 1 SMA (acute Werdnig-Hoffmann disease)
Type 2 SMA (chronic Werdnig-Hoffman or Dubowitz disease)
Type 3 SMA (Kugelberg-Welander disease)
Type 4 SMA

Classification
Type 0 SMA can be diagnosed prenatally by decreased fetal movement, and patients
often have congenital heart defects; it is historically fatal in the first week of life.
The onset of type 1 SMA occurs at birth and is characterized by severe involvement of
the spinal muscles. Children with type 1 SMA have poor head control, inability to sit, and
difficulty swallowing/feeding. Classic findings include tongue atrophy and fasciculation.
The intercostal muscle weakness that develops contributes to respiratory failure and
death by age 2 years.
The onset of type 2 SMA occurs at age 6 to 18 months and often is diagnosed by delayed
motor milestones. Function diminishes with time, with weakness being worse in the
lower extremities than in the upper extremities; however, children are able to sit
independently. Classic orthopaedic problems include hip dislocations, scoliosis, and joint
contractures, with life expectancy exceeding 20 years.
The onset of type 3 SMA is after age 18 months, with patients presenting with scoliosis,
hand tremors, and hip abductor weakness, resulting in a Trendelenburg gait. They can
stand independently and walk early but a progressive disease develops that ultimately
leads to wheelchair dependence as adults. Life expectancy is normal.
The onset of type 4 SMA occurs at an adult age (age >30 years) with moderate proximal
muscle weakness

Evaluation/Diagnosis
Patient History
Unless a positive family history of SMA exists, evaluation of a child for SMA is based on a
patient history, clinical findings of a physical examination, and the outcome of a genetic
workup.
Physical Examination
Hypotonia with progressive, symmetric, proximal more than distal muscle weakness that
spares the facial muscles but often has bulbar involvement
Joint evaluation with goniometer
Muscle strength
American Spinal Injury Association grading system (0 through 5)
Functional scale
Children’s Hospital of Philadelphia Infant Test of Neuromuscular Disorders
Hammersmith Functional Motor Scale Expanded
Revised Upper Limb Module
Motor Function Measure
Endurance
6-Minute Walk Test
Imaging Studies
Scoliosis
Sitting or standing PA/lateral scoliosis radiographs using slot-scanning, low-dose technology,
if possible
If the patient is unable to sit, a supine assessment of the spinal deformity is performed.
Ideally, serial radiographs should be obtained in the same fashion to gauge progression.
Hip subluxation/dislocation
AP pelvis radiograph in the supine position; account for hip flexion contracture by flexing the
contralateral hip
Diagnosis
SEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 9:40 AM
AAOS | Spinal Muscular Atrophy
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6002080
4/15

Quantitative analysis of SMN1 and SMN23
Multiplex ligation–dependent probe amplification
Quantitative polymerase chain reaction
Next-generation sequencing
Differential Diagnosis
Other diagnoses associated with weakness and low muscle tone must be considered. A
referral to genetics should be considered if the diagnosis is in question or diagnostic tests
need to be ordered or confirmed.
Management
Overview
Scoliosis is very common and progressive in patients with SMA (60% to 90%).4
Onset may be as early as 8 months of age, with the mean age of onset being between 6 and
8 years.
Nonsurgical management includes observation in patients with a Cobb angle less than 20°
and patients with type 1 SMA; however, this is being challenged given the response to
medical therapies.
For patients with type 2 or type 3 SMA who have a Cobb angle greater than 20° but less than
50° in patients, surgeons recommend bracing or seating supports with the use of rolls,
beanbags, molded pillows, or wedges.
Surgical treatment generally is considered for patients older than 4 years with a curve
greater than 50°; however, this remains controversial.5
Hip dislocation
May be unilateral or bilateral
Contractures
Lower extremity contractures are common in patients with SMA because of decreased range
of motion, prolonged static sitting position, and agonist-antagonist muscle imbalance.

Overview
SEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 9:40 AM
AAOS | Spinal Muscular Atrophy
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6002080
5/15

Radiographic examination is recommended based on the forward bending test
performed with the child sitting or standing in the most upright position attainable.
Progression of the deformity is faster in patients with the more severe types of SMA and
in patients who have stopped walking. In these patients, progression is at a rate of
approximately 10° per year. The curve type is most frequently thoracolumbar with pelvic
obliquity and hyperkyphosis. Robinson et al6 reported an inverse relationship between
pulmonary function test scores and the severity of scoliosis, with every 10° increase in
the Cobb angle correlating with a 3.3% decrease in peak flow and a 4.7% decrease in
predicted vital capacity. Weak intercostal muscles result in bell-shaped ribs that decline
and ultimately collapse, referred to as the parasol deformity, ultimately compromising
the space available for the lungs at the apex (Figure 1).
SEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 9:40 AM
AAOS | Spinal Muscular Atrophy
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6002080
6/15

Figure 1 AP supine radiograph of a spine demonstrates downward sloping of the ribs on
the left side of the thoracic cage. This phenomenon is referred to as the parasol rib
deformity, which is thought to result from the weak intercostal muscles in patients with
an overpowering diaphragm. (Courtesy of Jason B. Anari, MD, Philadelphia, PA.)
The presence of pain should be the main indication for management and may require
release of the hip adductor and flexor and/or osteotomies to maintain reduction of hip
dislocation and minimize symptoms. The management of hip dysplasia and instability in
patients with SMA is controversial but may become a more viable treatment option as
function improves with the use of biologics.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 9:40 AM
AAOS | Spinal Muscular Atrophy
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6002080
7/15

Hip and knee contractures exceeding 30° to 40° generally are not managed surgically.
Occasionally, hamstring lengthening may be considered for contractures smaller than
these values in patients who are strong enough and have a strong motivation to walk.
Foot deformities, such as equinovarus, commonly occur in patients with SMA. Rarely, if a
patient is ambulatory and retains strength, tenotomy of the gastrocnemius-soleus,
posterior tibialis, flexor digitorum longus, and flexor hallucis longus tendons may be
performed to maintain standing and walking. The key concept is that contractures
causing pain or limiting function can be managed surgically. Difficulty in shoeing or
hygiene issues are other indications for surgical management of limb and foot
deformities.
Nonsurgical Management
Use of a thoracolumbosacral orthosis in patients with SMA is controversial.
Nusinersen
Onasemnogene abeparvovec-xioi
Risdiplam

Nonsurgical Management
The historic literature suggests that a rigid thoracolumbosacral orthosis interferes with
pulmonary function by constricting the chest.7 A survey of surgeons who manage
scoliosis in patients with SMA suggest that a thoracolumbosacral orthosis improves
sitting balance given the hypotonic trunk but does not stop progression of the disease.8
Therefore, soft and rigid orthoses are used given lack of consensus. Sporadic reports of
slowing the progression of deformity occur with bracing.9 The initiation of treatment
occurs with a Cobb angle greater than 20°, with monitoring every 6 months until skeletal
maturity and annually after cessation of skeletal growth. If bracing is recommended,
orthotists must create a large abdominal window for the gastrostomy tube and ease of
respiration.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 9:40 AM
AAOS | Spinal Muscular Atrophy
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6002080
8/15

Nusinersen was the first drug to receive approval by the FDA for the management of
SMA.10 Nusinersen must be administered via an intrathecal route because it does not
cross the blood-brain barrier to act on the anterior horn cells. Nusinersen is an antisense
oligonucleotide that alters the splicing of SMN2 messenger RNA and increases the
amount of functional SMN protein produced. Nusinersen is more effective in patients
with infantile and childhood-onset SMA. A loading dose is administered, followed by
three doses annually for life. The 1-year cost of nusinersen is $750,000, with a
subsequent cost of $125,000 per injection. Recently, a subcutaneous intrathecal catheter
system was developed to allow for repeated outpatient dosing, even in patients with
spinal instrumentation.
Various approaches are available to treat patients with spinal instrumentation but still
provide access to the intrathecal space for the administration of nusinersen, including
skip segments11 or a laminectomy.12
Onasemnogene abeparvovec-xioi was the second drug to receive approval by the FDA
for the management SMA, originally approved for children older than 2 years.
Onasemnogene abeparvovec-xioi is a single-dose drug administered intravenously. The
drug is an adeno-associated viral vector that uses gene therapy to replace the SMN1
gene. Onasemnogene abeparvovec-xioi is the most expensive treatment option in the
world, costing $2,125,000.
Risdiplam recently received approval by the FDA for the management of SMA in children
older than 2 months. The unique aspect is that risdiplam is administered orally. The drug
increases exon 7 inclusion in SMN2 messenger RNA and full-length SMN2 protein
production in the brain. The drug cost is weight based and capped to be no more than
$340,000 per year.
Surgical Management
Scoliosis Indications
Cobb angle greater than 50° that is progressive, causing pain, contributing to poor sitting
balance, causing decubiti, or causing thoracic insufficiency syndrome
SEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 9:40 AM
AAOS | Spinal Muscular Atrophy
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6002080
9/15

Other surgical factors include declining respiratory function, parasol rib deformity,
hyperkyphosis, pelvic obliquity, truncal imbalance, and impairment of functional mobility.

Scoliosis Indications
In a child who is extremely young (<4 years) and has a curve that remains flexible, many
surgeons prefer to wait and follow the annual rate of progression per year, curve
magnitude, and curve flexibility before proceeding with growth-friendly instrumentation.
In children older than 4 years but younger than 10 years, growth-friendly
instrumentation (vertical expandable prosthetic titanium rib, magnetically controlled
growing rod, traditional growing rod, or Shilla procedure) is used to correct deformity
but allow for continued spinal growth. In patients older than 10 years, posterior spine
fusion is performed with segmental pedicle screw instrumentation; anterior procedures
rarely are necessary. Instrumentation to the pelvis is included if the spinal deformity
includes the pelvis. Skeletal maturity markers (triradiate cartilage, Risser sign, Sanders
bone age) are used in addition to chronologic age to determine if a patient is a candidate
for a single final fusion.
Pulmonary function tests should be included in the preoperative evaluation to assess
risk and help guide postoperative management. Parasol rib deformity is not addressed
via any of the previously mentioned spinal treatment options. Ongoing research is
examining the role such collapse plays in the development of restrictive lung disease
that ultimately leads to respiratory decline.13 Preoperatively, the family must be
counseled about decreased upper extremity function after posterior spine fusion given
the rigid trunk. Informing the patient that activities of daily living can be maintained via
adaptive occupational therapy devices is critical. Surgical management may result in an
ambulatory child losing the ability to walk because curve progression coincides with
disease worsening.
Techniques/Procedures
Preoperative Planning
SEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 9:40 AM
AAOS | Spinal Muscular Atrophy
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6002080
10/15

Poor bone quality likely because of decreased loading and abnormal bony morphology makes
standard posterior instrumentation with the use of pedicle screws difficult.
In patients with thin paraspinal musculature and a poor soft-tissue envelope, prominent
implants often are problematic.
Surgical Approach
Unique to SMA is the need to create a window to the intrathecal space in patients with spinal
instrumentation (Figures 2 and 3).
Figure 2 Preoperative (A) and postoperative (B) AP radiographs of the spine of a 12-year-old girl
with SMA2. (Images courtesy of Jason Anari, MD, Philadelphia, PA.)
SEND FEEDBACK

11/15

Figure 3 Intraoperative photograph of the spine of the patient in Figure 2 shows posterior spine
instrumentation and fusion from T3 through L5. Note the laminectomy performed to achieve
intrathecal access for the administration of nusinersen protected by fat graft. (Image courtesy of
Jason Anari, MD, Philadelphia, PA.)
Complications
Proximal and distal anchor failure, infection, skin breakdown secondary to prominent
hardware, junction deformities, and global malalignment are complications in patients with
SMA who have scoliosis.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 9:40 AM
AAOS | Spinal Muscular Atrophy
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6002080
12/15

Such complications also can occur in patients with growing instrumentation or patients who
have undergone a final fusion.
Outcomes
Classic literature reports improvement in postoperative peak flow and vital capacity with a
slower loss of pulmonary function in patients with SMA after arthrodesis.14-16
Early reports on growing constructs (most recently the magnetically controlled growing rod)
suggest a promising treatment modality for patients with SMA; however, longer term follow-up
is necessary.5,16
Mark as Complete
